what_its_for: Trientine is used to treat Wilson's disease, a rare condition where your body stores too much copper. It works by binding to extra copper in your body and helping your kidneys remove it through your urine. It is usually used in people who cannot tolerate penicillamine, another medicine for Wilson's disease.
how_to_take: Take trientine by mouth on an empty stomach, at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals and any other medicines, vitamins, or supplements. Swallow the capsules or tablets whole — do not crush, chew, or open them. Take it with a full glass of water. Space your doses evenly throughout the day. Wash your hands after handling the capsules, as the contents can irritate your skin.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your age, weight, and how well your body responds to treatment. Adults usually start with 750 mg to 1,250 mg per day, divided into 2 to 4 doses. Children typically start with 500 mg to 750 mg per day, divided into 2 to 4 doses. Your doctor may adjust your dose over time. Never change your dose without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — unless it is almost time for your next dose. In that case, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do not double up or take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store trientine in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C and 8°C). Keep it in the original container with the cap tightly closed. Protect it from moisture and light. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not use after the expiration date printed on the package. Ask your pharmacist how to safely dispose of any unused medicine.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking trientine at the same time as iron supplements, zinc supplements, antacids, vitamins, or other minerals, as these can block trientine from working properly — space them apart by at least 2 hours. Avoid eating or drinking (except water) close to the time you take your dose. Avoid breaking open the capsules, as the powder can irritate your skin, eyes, and mouth. Talk to your doctor before starting any new medicines, vitamins, or supplements.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away if you notice: signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, hives, itching, swelling of your face or throat, or trouble breathing; unusual bruising or bleeding; fever, chills, or signs of infection; muscle weakness or cramps; numbness or tingling in your hands or feet; yellowing of your skin or eyes (jaundice); dark urine; stomach pain; worsening of your neurological symptoms such as tremors or difficulty speaking; or any other new or worsening symptoms that concern you.
when_it_works: Trientine begins working to remove excess copper from your body fairly quickly, but you may not notice improvements in your symptoms right away. It can take several weeks to months before you start feeling better. Regular blood and urine tests will help your doctor see how well the medicine is working. It is very important to keep taking trientine every day, even if you feel well, because Wilson's disease requires lifelong management.
special_populations: Pregnant women: Talk to your doctor right away if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Trientine may be needed during pregnancy since untreated Wilson's disease can be dangerous to both mother and baby, but your doctor will carefully monitor you and may adjust your dose. Breastfeeding: It is not known if trientine passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Children: Trientine can be used in children, but the dose will be lower and adjusted based on your child's weight. Children should be closely monitored by their doctor. Older adults: Use with caution; your doctor may monitor you more closely for side effects.
